note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

traditional.note: The varṇamālā as a pandit recites it — the pronunciation the śikṣā treatises describe and Sanskrit recitation has carried unbroken. Lekha reads Devanagari, but reads it as Hindi, so four Hindi habits are worked around throughout. The name is given in its grammatical nominative (ककारः, not ककार) because Hindi deletes a word-final inherent a and the visarga blocks that deletion, restoring the final vowel Sanskrit requires — this is not a trick but what a grammarian actually says for 'the letter ka'. ऋ ॠ ऌ ॡ are handed to Czech and Slovak, the only installed languages with syllabic liquids, and Slovak alone with long ones. ऐ and औ are respelt आइ and आउ, their classical analysis as ā+i and ā+u, because Hindi has flattened them to [ɛː] and [ɔː]. And ष goes to a Russian voice, the only one that can make it audibly different from श. Two further signs are borrowed: ङ from Indonesian and ञ from Spanish, both for word-initial nasals Hindi cannot begin a word with. One caveat that applies to every Lekha clip here and cannot be tested by ear from this machine: if the voice drops the final visarga instead of sounding it, these fall back to the plain Hindi reading and the restored inherent vowel is lost.

0.why: Hindi अ is [ə] — the same obscure short vowel Sanskrit अ is, and precisely the hall's gloss, 'the u of but rather than the a of father'. The name frame is used rather than a bare अ because a lone vowel gives the synthesiser nothing to time against, and because अकारः set beside आकारः makes the length contrast audible as a contrast, in identical surroundings.
0.compromise: The final inherent a survives only because the name is put in the nominative, so the word ends '-raḥ' with a light breath that the hall's label 'akāra' does not show.

1.why: आकार is a real Hindi word — ākār, 'shape' — so the long [aː] is reliably long, and the opposition against अकारः is the single most robust vowel contrast Hindi has: schwa against long a.
1.compromise: The rate is left at default and deliberately not slowed. Slowing would stretch the whole word, so अ and आ would then differ in tempo as well as in vowel length, which is the wrong lesson. Hindi's own contrast already gives roughly the two-to-one ratio the hall states, but it is Hindi's ratio, not a measured one.

2.why: Devanagari इ read natively, in the frame that lets it be set against ईकारः.
2.compromise: Hindi's short इ is lax [ɪ] — the vowel of English 'sit', which is in fact what the hall states — where Sanskrit's is a short close [i]. So this pair differs in quality as well as in length, marginally more than it strictly should.

3.why: Hindi ई is a long tense [iː] — exactly the 'ee of see, held long' the hall asks for, and clearly distinct from इ in both length and tenseness.
3.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

4.why: Read natively, in the frame that lets it be set against ऊकारः.
4.compromise: As with इ: Hindi's short उ is lax [ʊ], the u of 'put' — the hall's own gloss — where Sanskrit's is a short close [u]. Quality carries part of the contrast that should be carried by length alone.

5.why: Hindi ऊ is a long tense [uː], the 'oo of food' held, and audibly the long partner of उ.
5.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

6.why: The one sound Lekha certainly gets wrong: Hindi reads ऋ as [rɪ], which is the northern reading the hall names and which is offered under the other system. Czech is the nearest thing available to a true syllabic r — in 'rkára' the first syllable contains no vowel, so Czech phonotactics force the r itself to be the nucleus, as in krk, prst, vlk. Czech á is a long [aː], Czech k is unaspirated, and the final -a is not deleted, so no visarga is needed.
6.compromise: The Slavic syllabic r is an alveolar trill held as a syllable; Sanskrit ऋ is classed retroflex (mūrdhanya) and in Indian recitation is closer to a syllabic [ɻ]. Czech stresses the first syllable, so the weight falls on the r rather than on the long ā where Sanskrit puts it. And the timbre is Czech, not Indian.

7.why: Slovak is the only installed language — very nearly the only language in Europe — with a phonemically LONG syllabic r, written ŕ as in vŕba. That is exactly what this sign is, and nothing else on this machine can produce it.
7.compromise: The rate is dropped as well, which lengthens the whole word rather than the liquid alone. Slovak's rhythmic law forbids ŕ and á in successive syllables, so 'ŕkára' is not a possible Slovak word: the voice is reading a spelling it has never met and may not honour both lengths. The hall notes this vowel is met almost nowhere outside genitive plurals like pitṝṇām.

8.why: Czech lkát, 'to sob', begins with precisely this syllable — a syllabic l with no vowel beside it, the hall's 'le of table said alone'. Hindi has no reading for ऌ whatever, and feeding Lekha the bare sign risks an artefact rather than a pronunciation.
8.compromise: Sanskrit ऌ is classed dental; Czech l is alveolar and somewhat dark. Czech initial stress again puts the weight on the liquid rather than on the long ā.

9.why: Slovak ĺ, as in kĺb and dĺžka, is a long syllabic l — the only one available anywhere on this machine, and the only way to make this sign audibly differ from ऌ.
9.compromise: The hall says plainly that this sound occurs in no Sanskrit word at all and is sustained only in reciting the alphabet. The clip is therefore a demonstration of a grammarians' construct, not of anything ever spoken. The reduced rate lengthens the whole word, not just the l. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

10.why: Hindi ए is a pure long [eː] with no off-glide — one of the few languages available that does not diphthongise this vowel. An English voice saying 'ay' would give [eɪ], which is exactly the glide the hall says to leave out.
10.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

11.why: The sign itself is unusable here: Hindi ऐ is the monophthong [ɛː], which the hall says outright ('northern speech flattens it toward the e of bed'). Respelt as आइ — the grammarians' own analysis of ai as ā + i, the vṛddhi grade — which Hindi reads as a genuine [aːɪ] sequence, as in आइए.
11.compromise: Hindi may render आइ as two syllables with a slight break rather than as one heavy diphthong. Whether classical ai was [aːi] or a lighter [ai] is itself answered by the grammarians with vowel-grade arithmetic rather than with a description of sound.

12.why: Hindi ओ is a pure long [oː], undiphthongised. An English 'oh' would give [əʊ] — again precisely the glide the hall says to omit.
12.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

13.why: As with ऐ: Hindi औ has flattened to [ɔː], so the sign cannot carry the classical value. Respelt आउ, the classical ā + u, which Hindi reads as a real [aːʊ] sequence.
13.compromise: Same as ऐ — the two elements may be heard as two syllables rather than as one diphthong, and the first element's length depends on Hindi's own timing rather than on a measured two morae.

14.why: Unlike every -kāra name, 'anusvāra' does not contain the sound it names. So the clip gives the sign as it is actually recited in the varṇamālā — aṃ — and then the name after it. Hindi's ं on a word-final vowel is a nasalisation of that vowel, which is one of the anusvāra's genuine values.
14.compromise: The anusvāra has no fixed place of articulation: it takes it from whatever follows, as the hall says. Any citation form is therefore one of its faces and not the sound itself. Before a pause the śikṣās describe a pure nasal resonance; Hindi may instead give an audible velar [ŋ].

15.why: As with the anusvāra, the recited sign first and the name after, because 'visarga' does not contain a visarga.
15.compromise: This is the worst clip in the hall and should be said to be. The defining feature of the visarga is the faint echo of the preceding vowel after the breath — the hall's own example, rāmaḥ ending 'raama-ha' — and Hindi does not do it: a word-final ः is read as a bare [h], and Hindi's h is voiced [ɦ] where the visarga is a voiceless outbreath. No installed voice can produce a tapering voiceless echo vowel; a Finnish or German 'aha' would give the shape but not the word, and was rejected for that reason.

16.why: Hindi initial क is genuinely unaspirated, because Hindi holds it in contrast with ख and so cannot blur them the way an English voice would. The hall asks for the k of 'skill', and this is it.
16.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

17.why: Hindi ख is a true aspirated [kʰ], and this is worth hearing immediately after ककारः: the fourfold stop contrast is the thing Indo-Aryan alone preserves, and no European voice on this machine can demonstrate it.
17.compromise: None of consequence. Some Hindi speech fricativises toward [x] in Perso-Arabic vocabulary, but that is written ख़ with a nuqta and should not touch this spelling — which is also why the hall's warning, 'never the ch of loch', is safe here.

18.why: Hindi ग is a plain voiced [ɡ], the g of 'go', with no fricative softening between vowels of the kind Spanish would impose.
18.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

19.why: The voiced aspirate — breathy-voiced [ɡʱ]. Hindi is the only language installed on this machine that has this series at all, which is exactly the hall's own point: every other surviving Indo-European branch merged or devoiced it.
19.compromise: None of consequence. The hall's gloss, 'doghouse run together', understates it: this is murmur through the whole release, not a stop followed by a separate h.

20.why: This velar nasal has to begin a word, and no European language permits that. Indonesian does, natively and constantly — 'ng' is unambiguously [ŋ] — and Indonesian also gives an unaspirated k, unreduced vowels, and a final vowel it does not delete. Lekha might well render ङ as [ŋ], but Hindi never begins a word with it (the hall says so: it stands only before another velar), and the gamble is not worth taking on the one sign whose entire content is that consonant.
20.compromise: Indonesian has no vowel length, so the ā of kāra is merely stressed, not long; both outer vowels are full [a] rather than the obscure [ɐ]; and Indonesian r is a trill where Sanskrit र is a tap. The consonant is right and the frame around it is approximate.

21.why: Hindi च is unaspirated and held apart from छ — the hall's 'ch of church but without the puff'. English has no unaspirated affricate to offer.
21.compromise: Hindi च is a postalveolar affricate [tʃ]; Sanskrit's is described as a palatal stop made with the tongue flat against the hard palate, a little less affricated and made with the blade rather than the tip.

22.why: Hindi छ is the aspirated partner of च, and the two clips together give one of the cleanest aspiration contrasts the voice can produce.
22.compromise: The same place-of-articulation approximation as च: postalveolar affricate rather than a flat palatal stop.

23.why: Hindi ज is [dʒ], voiced and unaspirated — the j of 'jam' the hall asks for.
23.compromise: As च: postalveolar rather than fully palatal.

24.why: The voiced palatal aspirate, again a sound only an Indo-Aryan voice possesses.
24.compromise: The hall calls झ the rarest of the palatals in classical Sanskrit, and it is not common in Hindi either, so Lekha has had correspondingly little material to learn it from; the breathy voicing may come out weaker than on भ or घ.

25.why: The hall's own gloss is 'ny as in Spanish señor', so the Spanish voice is taken at its word. Spanish supplies a clean [ɲ]; an unaspirated [k] from c before a; an intervocalic tap [ɾ], which is what Sanskrit र actually is; a final vowel it does not delete; and — because Spanish stresses the penultimate syllable of a vowel-final word — stress falling exactly on the -kā-. Hindi never begins a word with ञ, so Lekha is not asked to.
25.compromise: All three vowels are full Spanish [a]: Sanskrit's first and last should be the obscure short a and its second should be long, and Spanish marks that syllable by stress alone. The voice and timbre are Spanish.

26.why: Hindi has the retroflex series natively and unambiguously — tongue-tip curled back to the roof of the mouth, exactly as the hall describes. This is the other thing, besides the voiced aspirates, that no other voice on this machine can even approach.
26.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

27.why: The aspirated retroflex, native to Hindi and held in contrast with ट. Hearing टकारः and ठकारः back to back gives both the retroflexion and the aspiration in one comparison.
27.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

28.why: The voiced retroflex stop. Word-initial position matters here: Hindi turns ड into the flap ड़ [ɽ] between vowels, and the name form keeps it initial, where it stays a stop.
28.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

29.why: The voiced aspirated retroflex — retroflexion, voicing and murmur in a single segment, which is about as far from anything a European voice can do as this hall gets.
29.compromise: Between vowels Hindi would flap this to [ɽʱ]; putting the letter at the head of its own name is what keeps it a clean stop. The Vedic softening to ḷh that the hall mentions is not represented.

30.why: Standard Hindi maintains a distinct retroflex nasal, so Lekha can give [ɳ] where every other installed voice would give a plain n.
30.compromise: Casual Hindi speech leans ण toward a dental n, and a voice trained on modern read speech may retroflex it more lightly than a reciter of the Rāmāyaṇa would. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

31.why: Hindi त is a true dental with the tongue-tip on the upper teeth and unaspirated — the hall asks for the t of French 'tu', and Hindi's is if anything more firmly dental. An English voice would give an alveolar and aspirate it, producing neither त nor थ.
31.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

32.why: The aspirated dental. The hall warns it is never the th of 'thin'; a Hindi voice cannot make that mistake, because Hindi has no [θ] at all.
32.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

33.why: Voiced dental, as in the hall's Spanish 'donde' — and better than Spanish would give it, since Spanish would soften d to a fricative between vowels.
33.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

34.why: The voiced dental aspirate. The hall warns it is never the th of 'this', and Hindi keeps it a breathy-voiced stop rather than a fricative.
34.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

35.why: Hindi न is dental, with the tongue against the teeth, and audibly distinct from the retroflex ण two clips earlier.
35.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

36.why: Hindi initial प is unaspirated, because Hindi contrasts it with फ. The hall asks for the p of 'spin'; an English voice saying 'pa' would give [pʰ], which in this alphabet is a different letter.
36.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

37.why: Written without the nuqta, so that Hindi reads it as the native aspirated [pʰ] the hall calls for rather than as the [f] of loanwords, which is spelt फ़ and is what the modern system deliberately uses.
37.compromise: This is the least safe of the Lekha consonants. Modern Hindi speech leans on [f] even for native फ, and a voice trained on modern Hindi may follow it. If the clip sounds like 'fakāra', the synthesiser has done exactly what the hall warns modern speech does, and the classical value is not being heard.

38.why: A plain voiced [b], the b of 'bin', with no fricative softening.
38.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending. The manuscript confusion of ब with व that the hall notes is a scribal matter, not an audible one.

39.why: The voiced labial aspirate — the sound at the head of bhakti and bhagavat, and the clearest of the four murmured stops because the lips make the murmur easy to hear.
39.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

40.why: A plain [m]; nothing in Hindi disturbs it.
40.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

41.why: Hindi य is [j], the y of 'yes', word-initially and without the affrication some varieties impose.
41.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending.

42.why: Hindi र is a single alveolar tap — precisely the hall's 'single tap of the tongue, as in Italian caro'. An English voice would give an approximant, which is a different sound entirely.
42.compromise: The grammarians class र as retroflex (mūrdhanya); the Hindi tap is alveolar, made a little further forward than the tradition's own description implies.

43.why: Hindi ल is a clear l with none of the darkening an English voice would add before a back vowel.
43.compromise: Hindi's l is alveolar; Sanskrit's is classed dental, made with the tongue against the teeth. A small difference, and the only one here.

44.why: The Vedic retroflex lateral. The sign is written out and Lekha asked to read it, because no installed language has [ɭ] at the start of a word — Swedish and Norwegian have it only in rl clusters, and there is no Marathi voice on this machine.
44.compromise: Hindi does not use ळ. Lekha will most likely read it as a plain ल, in which case this clip is indistinguishable from लकारः and the retroflexion the sign exists to mark is simply absent. Treat it as a placeholder for a sound the machine cannot make.

45.why: Hindi व is [ʋ], a labiodental approximant standing exactly between v and w — which is word for word what the hall describes, and which neither English nor German nor Italian can supply.
45.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending. The clip cannot show the second half of the hall's description — that after another consonant व is heard as w, as in svāhā — because the letter stands alone here.

46.why: Hindi श is a clean [ʃ], the sh of 'ship'. In this system it is deliberately paired against a ष taken from a Russian voice, so that the two are audibly different — which the hall says is what pandits still maintain and most modern speech does not.
46.compromise: Hindi श is postalveolar [ʃ]; Sanskrit श is the palatal [ɕ], made with the blade raised to the hard palate rather than with the tongue drawn back behind the ridge. The cost of restoring the ś/ṣ contrast is that its two halves are spoken by two different voices in two different languages.

47.why: Hindi has merged ष into श, so Lekha would simply say श twice and the distinction the hall cares about would vanish. Russian ш is a genuine retroflex sibilant [ʂ], the only one installed. Russian fits the rest of the word better than it has any right to: unstressed /a/ reduces to [ɐ] before the stress and [ə] after it, which is exactly what Sanskrit's short a is, so ша-ка́-ра should land on [ʂɐˈkarə] — with the inherent final vowel intact and no visarga needed to hold it there.
47.compromise: The stress mark is written in, but Apple's Russian voice may not honour a combining acute; if the stress lands elsewhere the vowel reduction moves with it and the word is mangled. Russian has no phonemic vowel length, so kā is stressed rather than long. Russian ш is laminal where Sanskrit ष is apical. And this single letter is spoken by a different woman in a different language, which is audible.

48.why: Hindi स is a dental [s], made against the teeth as the hall specifies, and distinct from both श and the borrowed ष.
48.compromise: None of consequence beyond the nominative ending — though the nominative ending is itself a small irony here, since the hall notes that a word-final s becomes precisely that visarga.

49.why: The hall asks for an h that is voiced — 'the breath sounded rather than whispered' — and Hindi ह is exactly that, [ɦ]. An English or German h is voiceless and would be plainly wrong.
49.compromise: None of consequence. This is one of the few signs on which the living language and the grammarians agree completely.

modern.note: The same fifty signs read as a Hindi speaker reads them, which is how most of India pronounces the Sanskrit alphabet today. Nothing here is engineered: Lekha reading plain Devanagari simply IS this pronunciation. The final inherent a falls away, ऋ is [rɪ], ऐ and औ are the monophthongs [ɛː] and [ɔː], ष is merged into श, and फ is given its nuqta because modern speech makes it [f]. On some thirty consonants the two systems agree entirely and differ only in that dropped final vowel — that agreement is itself worth hearing, since it is what has been kept. The divergences are the short list the hall's own entries name: ri for ṛ, the flattened diphthongs, f for ph, the lost sibilant, and the letters ङ ञ ऌ ॡ ळ that Hindi has no living use for at all.

0.why: Devanagari read as Hindi, which is the whole method of this system. The short a is [ə], the same as Sanskrit's.
0.compromise: The final inherent a is deleted, as Hindi always deletes it word-finally: 'akār', not 'akāra'. That deletion is the single most pervasive difference between the two systems.

1.why: A real Hindi word — ākār, 'shape' — so the long vowel is beyond doubt. Hindi has kept the length contrast intact.

2.why: Hindi's short इ is the lax [ɪ] of 'sit', which is what the hall's own gloss describes.
2.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. The lax quality is Hindi's, slightly further from the close [i] a reciter would give.

3.why: Hindi ई is long and tense — the length contrast with इ is fully alive in the modern language.

4.why: Hindi's short उ is the lax [ʊ] of 'put', again matching the hall's gloss.

5.why: Long tense [uː], distinct from उ in both length and tenseness.

6.why: This is the northern reading the hall names outright: ऋ is sounded 'ri'. Nothing has to be engineered — Lekha does it by default, and that is exactly the point of this system. It is also why Kṛṣṇa reaches English as Krishna.
6.compromise: It is not a syllabic vowel at all but a consonant plus a vowel. The south says 'ru' instead, and neither reading is the vocalic r the grammarians describe; the traditional system borrows a Czech voice to get that.

7.why: Deliberately the short sign's spelling. Northern practice has no separate value for the long ॠ — it is read 'ri' like ऋ — and Hindi typography has so little use for the character that feeding it risks an artefact rather than a pronunciation.
7.compromise: This clip is identical to ऋकार, because in this pronunciation the two signs are identical. The length distinction survives only in the traditional reading, and the hall itself notes that ॠ is met almost nowhere outside forms like pitṝṇām. Modern Hindi has no length contrast for the vocalic r: ऋ and ॠ are both read [rɪ], so this clip is deliberately identical to ऋ. The distinction is real in Sanskrit and audible in the traditional reading.

8.why: ऌ is not part of the Hindi alphabet. When Hindi speakers read out the Sanskrit varṇamālā they say 'lṛ', which is spelt exactly this way — ल carrying the vocalic-r mātrā — and that is what this clip plays.
8.compromise: A consonant followed by [rɪ], not a syllabic l. The actual sign ऌ was not fed to the voice because Hindi TTS has no reliable mapping for it and the output would be an artefact rather than a pronunciation.

9.why: As ऌ: the practical northern reading, 'lṛ'.
9.compromise: Identical to ऌकार, because northern practice does not distinguish them — and the hall says this sound occurs in no Sanskrit word whatever, so there is nothing for a living pronunciation to be based on. This is the emptiest clip in the hall and the honest thing is to say so. As with ऋ/ॠ: Hindi has no length contrast here, so ऌ and ॡ are the same sound today and this clip is identical to ऌ.

10.why: Hindi ए is still a pure long [eː] with no glide, exactly as the classical language had it. Nothing has moved here.

11.why: The flattening the hall describes, heard directly: northern ऐ is the monophthong [ɛː], the e of 'bed' lengthened, and not a diphthong at all. Set this beside the traditional आइकारः and the whole distance is in one vowel.
11.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. Nothing else — this is simply what has become of the vowel.

12.why: Hindi ओ is still a pure long [oː], undiphthongised, as ए is. The mid vowels have held where the diphthongs have not.

13.why: As with ऐ: northern औ is the monophthong [ɔː] — the hall's 'aw' — where the classical value was ā + u.

14.why: The sign as recited, then its name, since the name does not contain the sound. Hindi's ं on a final vowel is nasalisation, and Hindi uses the anusvāra constantly, so this is well-trodden ground for the voice.
14.compromise: A citation form of a sound that has no citation form: the anusvāra takes its place of articulation from what follows it, so any isolated rendering is one face of it. The final a of अनुस्वार is deleted.

15.why: The sign, then its name. Hindi barely sounds a visarga — in दुःख it vanishes entirely, in प्रातः it survives as a light breath — and that is a fair representation of the modern reading.
15.compromise: Expect a light [h] or nothing at all. There is certainly no echo vowel, because modern Hindi has no use for one; so this is an accurate record of what has been lost and a poor demonstration of what the sound was.

16.why: Unaspirated [k], unchanged from the classical value — Hindi still holds it in contrast with ख.
16.compromise: Final inherent a deleted; otherwise identical to the traditional reading.

17.why: Aspirated [kʰ], kept. The fourfold stop system is the part of the inheritance Hindi has guarded most completely.

19.why: The breathy-voiced [ɡʱ] is fully alive in Hindi; this is one of the places the modern language has kept what Greek and Iranian both lost.
19.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. Some urban speech weakens the murmur, and a TTS voice trained on read speech may follow it.

20.why: Lekha is asked to read ङ directly, because the point of this system is what a Hindi speaker does with the sign. Hindi has [ŋ], but only before a velar — अंक, रंग — and never at the head of a word.
20.compromise: Whether the voice produces a real word-initial [ŋ] cannot be checked by ear from here; it may prefix a vowel or fall back on a plain n. The traditional system uses an Indonesian voice precisely to avoid this gamble, which is the honest measure of how uncertain this clip is.

21.why: Unaspirated [tʃ], unchanged from the traditional reading.
21.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. Postalveolar rather than flatly palatal, as in the traditional clip.

22.why: Aspirated [tʃʰ], kept in full contrast with च.

24.why: The voiced palatal aspirate survives in Hindi — jhaṇḍā, jhūṭh — though it is uncommon, as the hall says it was uncommon in classical Sanskrit too.
24.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. Being rare, it is the least well-trained of the four murmured stops and the breathiness may come out light.

25.why: Read directly. Hindi has [ɲ] only before palatals, as in पंच, and never initially, so this asks the voice for something Hindi does not do.
25.compromise: The same gamble as ङ: the voice may substitute a plain n. And the hall's own note shows how far this letter has drifted in the north — the cluster ज्ञ, which contains it, is read [ɡj] in Hindi, so ञ has effectively no independent life in the modern language.

26.why: The retroflex series is completely intact in Hindi — the one part of Sanskrit's consonant system that modern North India has not touched at all.
26.compromise: Final inherent a deleted; nothing else differs from the traditional reading.

27.why: Aspirated retroflex, intact. The hall notes it multiplied in the Prakrits; Hindi is where it ended up, and is thoroughly at home with it.

28.why: Voiced retroflex stop, intact, and initial here so it stays a stop rather than becoming Hindi's flap ड़.

29.why: Voiced aspirated retroflex, intact and initial.
29.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. Between vowels Hindi would flap this to [ɽʱ], which is the modern reflex of the same Vedic softening the hall describes — but the name form does not expose it.

30.why: Standard Hindi keeps the retroflex nasal distinct, so it is heard here as in the traditional reading.
30.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. In casual modern speech ण drifts toward a dental n, and the retroflexion may be lighter than a reciter's.

31.why: True dental, unaspirated, unchanged — Hindi has never let the dental and retroflex t collapse the way English does.

32.why: Aspirated dental, kept in contrast with त, exactly as the tradition guards it.

34.why: Voiced dental aspirate, alive and common in Hindi — dhan, dhūp, dharm.

35.why: Dental n, unchanged and distinct from ण.

36.why: Unaspirated [p], unchanged; Hindi still needs it to stay unaspirated in order to keep फ apart from it.

37.why: The nuqta is added deliberately, which makes Hindi read the letter as [f]. The hall says modern speech 'often makes it so'; this system makes that reading explicit rather than leaving it to the synthesiser's discretion, and sets it against the traditional [pʰ].
37.compromise: Not a compromise so much as a choice, and one that overstates the case slightly: careful Hindi speakers still say [pʰ] in native words such as phal, and the merger is a tendency rather than a completed change.

39.why: Voiced labial aspirate, entirely alive in Hindi and the easiest of the four murmured stops to hear.

42.why: A single alveolar tap, as in the classical language — the modern language has not weakened it to an approximant.
42.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. Alveolar rather than the retroflex the grammarians classed it as.

43.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. Alveolar rather than dental.

44.why: Read directly, though ळ is a Marathi and Vedic letter that Hindi does not use.
44.compromise: A Hindi speaker meeting ळ reads it as ल, and Lekha will almost certainly do the same, so this clip is probably indistinguishable from लकार. That is an accurate report of the modern reading and useless as a demonstration of the retroflex lateral — which survives, as the hall says, in Ṛgvedic recitation and in Marathi, neither of which is available here. ळ is not a letter of standard Hindi and has merged with ल, so this clip is identical to ल. It survives as a distinct sound in Marathi, Vedic recitation and several Dravidian languages.

45.why: Hindi व is [ʋ], between v and w, exactly as Sanskrit's was. Nothing has moved.

46.why: Hindi श is [ʃ], the sh of 'ship' — and in this system it is also what ष sounds like, which is the point of playing the two in succession.
46.compromise: Final inherent a deleted. Postalveolar [ʃ] rather than the palatal [ɕ] of the tradition.

47.why: Read directly — and Hindi reads ष as [ʃ], the same sound as श. That merger is the entire content of this clip.
47.compromise: This should sound identical to शकार, and that is not a defect. The hall says the distinction is one 'most modern Indian speech has let go', and this is what letting it go sounds like. The traditional system borrows a Russian voice to restore the retroflex sibilant; nothing in Hindi can. The श/ष merger is the best-known consonant merger in Modern Hindi: both are pronounced [ʃ], so this clip is identical to श. The tradition distinguishes palatal [ɕ] from retroflex [ʂ], and the traditional reading keeps them apart.

48.why: Dental [s], unchanged and still distinct from श — the one sibilant contrast Hindi has kept.

49.why: Hindi ह is voiced [ɦ], as Sanskrit's was — 'the breath sounded rather than whispered'. The last letter of the alphabet is also one of the few on which nothing at all has changed.
